title: Gen-PINNs: Generative Adversarial Physics Informed Neural Networks for solving partial differential equations
authors: Muhammad M. Akmal, Kamy Sepehrnoori, Michael J. Pyrcz
abstract: Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) are a widely used data-free method for solving Partial Differential Equations (PDEs) using machine learning. With recent advances in Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), adversarial learning has shown strong capabilities for modeling complex data-driven problems; however, the use of GANs in deterministic physics-informed PDE solutions remains limited. In this work, we first identify limitations of standard PINNs for solving PDEs, including spectral bias, loss imbalance, and optimizer stagnation. We then propose Generative Adversarial Physics-Informed Neural Networks (Gen-PINNs), a unified deterministic residual-adversarial framework designed to improve data-free solutions of PDEs with sharp or shock-front behavior. The generator learns the underlying PDE solution using dynamically weighted physics-informed loss components, while separate discriminators evaluate complementary PDE residual features against ideal zero-residual states. The framework further develops and adapts several methodological components, including a Fourier representation for resolving high-frequency spatial content, an orthonormal spectral diagnostic for quantifying frequency-dependent solution errors, and a modified gradient-based dynamic weighting system for physics, initial-condition, boundary-condition, and adversarial loss objectives. Gen-PINNs is tested against standard PINNs on nonlinear and higher-order PDEs, including the Burgers, Allen-Cahn, and Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equations. The results demonstrate substantial improvements in accuracy and convergence across sharp-front, stiff, and higher-order PDE solutions, highlighting the potential of deterministic residual-adversarial learning as an effective approach for solving challenging nonlinear PDEs.

infographic.key_insight: Gen-PINNs combines physics-informed learning with adversarial training to improve PDE solution quality where standard PINNs struggle with sharp gradients, spectral bias, and training imbalance.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This approach can improve data-free simulation of nonlinear fluid and wave-like systems that contain shocks, stiff dynamics, or high-frequency structure.
method: Generator learns PDE solutions with dynamically weighted physics, boundary, and initial-condition losses.
Discriminators enforce zero-residual behavior by judging complementary PDE residual features.
Fourier-based representation and spectral diagnostics help capture and evaluate high-frequency content.
infographic.evidence_signal: The method was evaluated against standard PINNs on the Burgers, Allen-Cahn, and Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equations, with reported gains in accuracy and convergence.
infographic.watch_item: The added adversarial and spectral components increase training complexity and may require careful tuning to avoid instability or imbalance.
infographic.paper_title: Gen-PINNs: Generative Adversarial Physics Informed Neural Networks for solving partial differential equations

title: On the relationships between pressure geometrization and vortex identification
authors: Han Tu, Hang Zhao, Qi Gao
abstract: The profound mathematical and conceptual analogy between pressure in fluid mechanics and gravity in general relativity motivates a novel geometric reinterpretation of flows. This article proposes a theoretical framework for geometrizing pressure by establishing a Newton-Cartan geometry and applying a conformal transformation to the spatial metric. The pressure field is reinterpreted as a geometric potential that induces an effective spatial curvature, encoded in the Ricci tensor Rij and the associated Einstein-like tensor Gij. Within this curved effective space, fluid particles under the exclusive influence of pressure follow geodesics, and the classical Euler equation is recovered in the weak-field limit. The pressure Poisson equation emerges naturally as a consequence of the geodesic equation and the Bianchi identity, revealing pressure as an instantaneous geometric constraint rather than an external force. This framework provides a unified geometric interpretation of widely used vortex identification criteria, demonstrating that the prevailing Eulerian and Lagrangian schemes correspond to different geometric invariants or projections of the effective curvature. In the degenerate two-dimensional (2D) limit, the effective spatial tensor vanishes identically, and the global integral of the total curvature vanishes as well. This topological constraint offers a novel interpretation of the dual-cascade scenario in 2D turbulence: the inverse energy cascade arises from geometric condensation of positive-curvature structures toward larger scales, while the forward enstrophy cascade results from geometric dispersion of negative-curvature structures toward smaller scales.

infographic.key_insight: Pressure can be treated as a geometric field that curves an effective spatial metric, making pressure-driven motion equivalent to geodesic flow and linking vortex criteria to curvature invariants.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This offers a unified geometric framework for interpreting turbulence diagnostics and could improve the physical consistency of vortex identification in CFD and flow analysis.
method: Build a Newton-Cartan geometric formulation of fluid flow.
Apply a conformal transformation to map pressure into effective spatial curvature.
Relate vortex identification criteria to Eulerian/Lagrangian geometric invariants and curvature projections.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a theoretical derivation, including recovery of the Euler equation in the weak-field limit and consistency with the pressure Poisson equation and Bianchi identity, rather than a data-driven benchmark.
infographic.watch_item: The framework is highly theoretical and may be difficult to validate or apply robustly in noisy experimental or high-Reynolds-number simulation data.
infographic.paper_title: On the relationships between pressure geometrization and vortex identification

title: Cova-PINN: Cross-Domain Conservation Physics-Informed Neural Network for Fluid-Solid Conjugate Heat Transfer in Complex Geometries
authors: Weizheng Zhang, Xunjie Xie, Hao Pan, Lin Lu
abstract: Multi-domain physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) flexibly model medium-specific representations to solve fluid--solid conjugate heat transfer (CHT). However, standard multi-domain PINNs enforce governing equations and interface conditions on separately sampled domain supports, which can yield plausible temperature fields but inaccurate end-to-end energy transfer and outlet temperatures. We propose Cova-PINN, a multi-domain PINN framework that aligns conservation support with thermal interaction paths in complex geometries. Cova-PINN jointly optimizes cross-domain composite control-volume balances at the local scale and paired-wall closure at the global exchanger scale. We evaluate Cova-PINN on four triply periodic minimal surface (TPMS) heat exchangers and a geometrically distinct DualMS design against CHT-specific, optimization-oriented, and complex-geometry PINN baselines under a common protocol. Relative to the closest baseline, MUSA-PINN-CHT, Cova-PINN reduces average outlet-temperature and device-level closure errors across the four TPMS topologies by $37.7\%$ and $60.2\%$, respectively, while also improving full-field and heat-duty accuracy, with consistent gains on DualMS.

infographic.key_insight: Cova-PINN improves fluid-solid conjugate heat transfer prediction by enforcing conservation across thermal interaction paths, not just within separately sampled fluid and solid domains.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method is especially relevant for heat exchangers and other complex geometries where accurate outlet temperature and end-to-end energy balance matter more than visually plausible temperature fields.
method: Cross-domain composite control-volume balances are optimized at the local scale.
Paired-wall closure is enforced at the global exchanger scale.
Multi-domain PINN supports medium-specific representations while aligning conservation with heat-transfer pathways.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluated on four TPMS heat exchangers and a DualMS design, Cova-PINN outperformed baselines under a common protocol, reducing average outlet-temperature and device-level closure errors by 37.7% and 60.2% versus the closest baseline.
infographic.watch_item: The approach adds conservation constraints tied to geometry and wall pairing, so performance may depend on correct path definitions and careful formulation for new exchanger layouts.
infographic.paper_title: Cova-PINN: Cross-Domain Conservation Physics-Informed Neural Network for Fluid-Solid Conjugate Heat Transfer in Complex Geometries

title: SAGE-PINN: A Singularity-free Axisymmetric Geometry-Encoded Physics-Informed Neural Network for Axisymmetric Multiphysics Flow in Cylindrical Coordinates
authors: Raj Maurya, Joyprakash Akhuli, Doyel Pandey
abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) provide a mesh-free framework for multiphysics modeling, yet fluid flow in axisymmetric cylindrical coordinates remains largely unexplored because the governing operators are singular at the axis and momentum and energy are strongly coupled through advection and buoyancy. We introduce SAGE-PINN, a Singularity-free Axisymmetric Geometry-Encoded Physics-Informed Neural Network for this class of problems. SAGE-PINN removes the coordinate singularity by construction: the parity-preserving variable $s=r^2$ and a modified stream-function representation eliminate explicit $1/r$ terms from the trained residuals and satisfy mass conservation identically. Boundary-fitted analytical ansätze enforce the boundary conditions exactly, while staged momentum-thermal-joint training, residual normalization, Péclet- and Richardson-number continuation, and a physics-scaled drift guard stabilize the coupled optimization. The framework is trained without labelled data, using only physics and boundary constraints, and its predictions are validated against finite-element reference solutions for steady nanofluid flow and heat transfer through a stenosed artery over a wide range of flow and thermal regimes, without case-specific tuning. Mass conservation remains at single-precision round-off, and over the central operating range the axial velocity and temperature are reproduced within $1.6\%$ and $9.1\%$ relative $L_2$ error, respectively. The main deterioration occurs only in the limiting regimes of strongly buoyancy-influenced slow flow and highly advection-dominated heat transfer. Embedding cylindrical geometry, conservation structure, and boundary physics directly into the network provides a robust route to PINN simulation of axisymmetric multiphysics flows.

infographic.key_insight: SAGE-PINN embeds axisymmetric cylindrical geometry and conservation laws directly into a PINN to remove the axis singularity and learn multiphysics flow without labeled data.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables mesh-free surrogate modeling for stenosed-artery-like axisymmetric flows and heat transfer, with stable physics-consistent predictions across changing buoyancy and advection regimes.
method: Use parity-preserving variable s = r^2 and a modified stream-function to eliminate explicit 1/r singular terms.
Enforce boundary conditions exactly with analytical, boundary-fitted ansätze.
Stabilize training with staged momentum-thermal-joint optimization, residual normalization, continuation in Péclet/Richardson numbers, and a physics-scaled drift guard.
infographic.evidence_signal: Validated against finite-element reference solutions for steady nanofluid flow and heat transfer, achieving single-precision mass conservation and central-range errors of 1.6% in axial velocity and 9.1% in temperature.
infographic.watch_item: Accuracy degrades in the most difficult regimes: strongly buoyancy-driven slow flow and highly advection-dominated heat transfer.
infographic.paper_title: SAGE-PINN: A Singularity-free Axisymmetric Geometry-Encoded Physics-Informed Neural Network for Axisymmetric Multiphysics Flow in Cylindrical Coordinates

title: Only Linear Constraints Survive Coarse-Graining: Evaluating Physics-Constrained Neural Operators on Stochastically Forced Turbulence
authors: Michael Groom, Rafael Oliveira
abstract: A physics-informed loss adds a discretised PDE residual to the data term, but is only strictly valid if the equations being enforced are closed on the fields being fitted. This fails on coarse-grained, stochastically forced data: nonlinear terms in the PDE generally do not commute with the filter, so the coarse-grained fields do not satisfy the original equations, and driving their residual to zero encodes an implicit closure into the learned operator. Under normalised, translation-invariant filtering on a periodic domain, constant-coefficient linear constraints remain valid on the filtered grid. For the 2D incompressible Navier-Stokes equations, two such constraints are continuity and global momentum balance. We enforce these exactly by applying a closed-form projection on the output of a Fourier neural operator (FNO) at $O(N \log N)$ cost. On two-dimensional isotropic turbulence, truncated so that its forcing lies entirely beyond the cutoff wavenumber, the projection achieves a continuity error of $5.0\times10^{-7}$ against 0.51 for a plain FNO and 0.17 for a physics-informed FNO, and a global momentum balance error of $8.6\times10^{-11}$ against $7.5\times10^{-4}$ and $8.3\times10^{-4}$. The projection only costs an extra 2% of training time, and takes the fraction of rollouts whose energy remains bounded at 448 steps from 0.18 to 0.87. On resolved Kolmogorov flow, test-time optimisation costs approximately 3,300$\times$ as much per trajectory as the projection, while leaving maximum divergence three orders of magnitude higher. Nonlinear constraints can also be enforced once their unclosed terms are modelled: closing the global energy balance with a constant subgrid flux, fitted from the coarse training data alone, removes the 20.9% energy deficit that enforcing the unclosed balance produces and keeps every free-running rollout bounded over 2,000 steps.

infographic.key_insight: Only constraints that remain closed after coarse-graining can be enforced exactly; for turbulence, linear constraints like incompressibility and global momentum survive filtering, while nonlinear PDE residuals can inject a wrong implicit closure.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For neural operators on coarse turbulent data, a simple Fourier-space projection can enforce physically valid constraints cheaply and improve long-horizon stability far more reliably than a full physics-informed residual.
method: Train a Fourier neural operator (FNO) on coarse turbulence fields.
Apply a closed-form O(N log N) projection to enforce continuity and global momentum exactly.
Optionally fit a constant subgrid flux to close the global energy balance on coarse data.
infographic.evidence_signal: On 2D isotropic turbulence, the projection reduced continuity error to 5.0e-7 and momentum-balance error to 8.6e-11, while increasing bounded 448-step rollouts from 0.18 to 0.87; on resolved Kolmogorov flow, test-time optimization was ~3300× more expensive than projection.
infographic.watch_item: The approach relies on identifying constraints that stay valid under filtering; enforcing unclosed nonlinear balances without modeling subgrid effects can hard-code an incorrect closure into the learned operator.
infographic.paper_title: Only Linear Constraints Survive Coarse-Graining: Evaluating Physics-Constrained Neural Operators on Stochastically Forced Turbulence

title: PoreML: A Data-Driven Framework for Learning Multiphase Flow in Porous Media
authors: Chunyang Wang, Mingrui Zhang, Yuyan Zhang, Linqi Zhu, Xin Ju, Edo Sicco Boek
abstract: Multiphase flow in porous microstructures is central to CO$_2$ storage, fuel-cell operation, and flip-chip packaging. Predicting these flows remains challenging because wettability and complex pore geometry govern the nonlinear evolution of fluid interfaces. Machine learning holds substantial promise for advancing the field, but progress is constrained by scarce time-resolved 3D datasets and a lack of a unified workflow for training and evaluating models. To fill this critical gap, we introduce PoreML, an open-source framework unifying data generation, model training, and evaluation grounded in pore-scale physics. The framework comprises three core components. (a) A modern GPU-native lattice Boltzmann solver, validated against analytical solutions and published experiments, enables reproducible data generation. (b) A 3.3 TB dataset contains 560 simulation runs and 158,546 stored time steps across four application-driven scenarios. These trajectories span synthetic structures and geometries derived from micro-CT scans of real materials, covering diverse wetting conditions and viscosity ratios. (c) A unified learning framework evaluates one-step prediction and autoregressive rollouts. Its domain-specific evaluation protocols assess predictive accuracy and physical consistency. We evaluate five models of diverse architecture under these protocols. Two complementary challenges assess transfer to larger domains and from synthetic to micro-CT-derived structures. PoreML provides a shared foundation for machine-learning research on multiphase flow in porous media, with the aim of empowering the community to develop reliable predictive models and advance the field.

infographic.key_insight: PoreML unifies porous-media data generation, model training, and evaluation to enable reliable machine-learning prediction of multiphase flow in complex pore geometries.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework supports better design and forecasting for applications such as CO2 storage, fuel cells, and packaging by providing reproducible pore-scale simulation data and benchmark tests.
method: GPU-native lattice Boltzmann solver for reproducible pore-scale data generation
3.3 TB dataset with 560 runs and 158,546 time steps across four scenarios
Unified evaluation for one-step prediction, autoregressive rollout, and physical consistency
infographic.evidence_signal: The benchmark includes five model architectures and two transfer tests, spanning larger domains and synthetic-to-micro-CT generalization.
infographic.watch_item: Performance may still be sensitive to domain shift, especially when transferring models to larger geometries or real micro-CT-derived structures.
infographic.paper_title: PoreML: A Data-Driven Framework for Learning Multiphase Flow in Porous Media

title: Net drag reduction in turbulent pipe flow by airfoil-section grids concentrated near the wall
authors: Takuya Masuda
abstract: The frictional drag of turbulent pipe flow is responsible for enormous energy consumption in water and natural gas distribution systems. Flow straighteners can reduce this drag by suppressing turbulence, but they generally induce a pressure loss that exceeds the reduction; similarly, large-eddy breakup devices installed in pipes have not achieved a net drag reduction. In this study, a grid of NACA0006 airfoils was adopted as a flow straightener to suppress the pressure loss, and its net drag reduction was evaluated by numerical simulations using the $k$-$ω$ shear stress transport model of the axisymmetric Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes equations with periodic boundary conditions. The model was validated against fully developed turbulent pipe flow and a previous experiment on a large-eddy breakup device in a pipe. Under a pressure difference corresponding to a Reynolds number ($\mathit{Re}$) of approximately $10^5$, a grid pattern of concentric rings concentrated near the wall at an axial spacing of 0.5 m increased the flow rate by up to 9.0%, and the flow rate increase remained positive for $5 \times 10^{4} \leq \mathit{Re} \leq 2 \times 10^{5}$. The grid pattern reduced the area-integrated Reynolds shear stress by 29% and brought the velocity profile closer to a laminar one. The effectiveness of the near-wall placement is consistent with the Fukagata-Iwamoto-Kasagi identity, which weights the Reynolds shear stress more heavily closer to the wall.

infographic.key_insight: Near-wall concentric airfoil grids can suppress turbulence enough to produce net drag reduction in a pipe, boosting flow rate by up to 9.0% at Re ≈ 10^5.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This suggests a passive flow-straightening design that could reduce pumping power in water and gas pipelines without the usual net-loss penalty of internal devices.
method: Axisymmetric RANS simulations with the k-ω SST turbulence model
Periodic boundary conditions in a pipe-flow configuration
Validated against fully developed turbulent pipe flow and prior large-eddy breakup device data
infographic.evidence_signal: At a pressure difference corresponding to Re ≈ 10^5, the best near-wall grid pattern increased flow rate by up to 9.0%, reduced area-integrated Reynolds shear stress by 29%, and stayed beneficial from 5×10^4 to 2×10^5.
infographic.watch_item: Results are based on RANS modeling, so experimental verification and sensitivity to real pipe roughness, fabrication tolerances, and pressure-loss penalties are important before deployment.
infographic.paper_title: Net drag reduction in turbulent pipe flow by airfoil-section grids concentrated near the wall

title: The binormal flow: a toy model for turbulence
authors: Elena Danesi, Pablo Merino, Luis Vega
abstract: These notes summarize the content of a one-week course given by Luis Vega on the binormal flow model applied to describe the dynamics of three-dimensional vortex filaments in incompressible fluids following the Euler equations. This topic touches connections between the binormal flow, the Schrödinger map and the 1d cubic nonlinear Schrödinger equation, providing a rich casuistry linked to the physical and numerical phenomenology. This course was part of the $2^{\text{nd}}$ Advanced Summer School held at the Institut d'Etudes Scientifiques de Cargèse (IESC), at Cargèse (Corsica), from $20^{\text{th}}$ to $30^{\text{th}}$ June 2023. These notes have been written and completed by two of its attendees, Elena Danesi and Pablo Merino.

infographic.key_insight: The binormal flow serves as a reduced toy model linking vortex-filament dynamics in 3D incompressible fluids to the Schrödinger map and 1D cubic nonlinear Schrödinger equation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It offers a mathematically tractable framework for understanding filament evolution, singularity formation, and turbulence-like behavior in fluid simulations.
method: Model 3D vortex filaments using the binormal flow approximation.
Exploit the equivalence to the Schrödinger map and 1D cubic NLS.
Use the model to interpret physical and numerical phenomenology of filament dynamics.
infographic.evidence_signal: The paper is a course-based review and synthesis rather than a new data-driven evaluation, grounded in theoretical connections and phenomenology discussed in the abstract.
infographic.watch_item: Because it is an idealized reduced model, results may not transfer directly to full 3D turbulent flows without careful validation.
infographic.paper_title: The binormal flow: a toy model for turbulence

title: Extending convolutional neural networks to finite-volume meshes for fine-scale reconstruction of wall-bounded turbulence
authors: Hesam Tofighian, Jordan A. Denev, Nikolai Kornev
abstract: Standard convolutional neural networks for turbulence super-resolution are restricted to uniform structured grids, preventing their direct application to the non-uniform and non-orthogonal meshes commonly used in wall-bounded flows and complex geometries. We introduce a finite-volume convolution unit (FVCU) that removes this restriction. The key idea is to construct convolutional layers using finite-volume operators that are applicable to non-uniform and unstructured meshes. To this end, we use an exact representation of a 3D convolution as a linear combination of successive axis-wise convolutions. We adopt axis-wise gradient, averaging, and identity operators, as they can be evaluated on arbitrary polyhedral cells using finite-volume discretization. The resulting FVCU is well-defined on general meshes, serving as a drop-in replacement for conventional convolution layers. The FVCU is embedded in a super-resolution neural network and trained to reconstruct 3D velocity fields from $4\times$ coarsened low-resolution fields in turbulent channel flow on a non-uniform mesh, and in circular-pipe flow on a non-orthogonal O-grid mesh. Inspired by the role of the Van Driest damping function in near-wall subgrid-scale modelling in large-eddy simulations, this function is supplied as a conditional input to encode wall proximity. An ablation study confirms that the network interprets this input in a physically consistent manner. In both configurations, the model accurately reconstructs instantaneous velocity fields, Reynolds-stresses and their anisotropy, and energy spectra beyond the Nyquist limit of the low-resolution mesh. On an elliptic pipe unseen during training, the model reproduces the main flow features and local statistics, with a modest overprediction of small-scale energy. These results demonstrate a framework for extending CNN-based super-resolution to general finite-volume grids.

infographic.key_insight: A new finite-volume convolution unit lets CNN super-resolution work directly on non-uniform, non-orthogonal meshes by replacing standard grid-based convolutions with finite-volume operators.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This makes turbulence reconstruction methods usable on the kinds of meshes actually employed in wall-bounded and complex-geometry CFD simulations.
method: Builds convolution from exact axis-wise decompositions of 3D convolution
Uses finite-volume gradient, averaging, and identity operators so layers work on arbitrary polyhedral cells
Adds Van Driest damping as a wall-proximity conditioning input
infographic.evidence_signal: The model was trained and evaluated on 4× coarsened channel-flow and pipe-flow data, accurately recovering velocity fields, Reynolds stresses, anisotropy, and energy spectra beyond the coarse-grid Nyquist limit, with additional tests on an unseen elliptic pipe.
infographic.watch_item: Performance is slightly weaker on the unseen elliptic pipe, with modest overprediction of small-scale energy, so generalization to new geometries and mesh types still needs careful validation.
infographic.paper_title: Extending convolutional neural networks to finite-volume meshes for fine-scale reconstruction of wall-bounded turbulence

title: Particle dynamics in a microfluidic T-junction vortex flow: the role of history force
authors: Matteo Chiatto, Luigi de Luca, Howard A. Stone, Francesco Grasso
abstract: The motion of inertial particles suspended in a carrier fluid, together with the dynamics of the underlying vortical structures, is investigated in a square microfluidic T-junction. The coherent structures forming near the branching strongly affect the particle distribution and may promote particle trapping around the T-region. Single-phase numerical simulations of the unperturbed base flow are combined with integration of the particle force balance equation, which, unlike most previous studies, includes the Basset-Boussinesq (BB) history force. The flow topology is analysed for $Re=500$ and $570$, while particle properties are varied through the Stokes number $St$ and the particle-to-fluid density ratio $ρ$. At $Re=500$ the base flow exhibits a steady vortex pair, whereas at $Re=570$ a Hopf bifurcation gives rise to a helical oscillation of the primary vortex pair characterized by periodic breathing. The BB history force has a non-negligible impact over the whole range of $(ρ, St)$ pairs investigated. It acts as an additional viscous force which, together with the drag of the relative motion, opposes the pressure-gradient force, widening particle spiral trajectories radially and elongating them axially. Its inclusion reduces the basin of attraction, indicating that memory effects promote particle displacement away from the vortex core and weaken trapping. At $Re=570$, spectral proper orthogonal decomposition characterizes the breathing of the primary vortex pair. Particles injected at a given location interact with the vortical structure at different phases of the cycle depending on the injection time, producing substantially different trajectories. This phase dependence is reflected in the shape and extent of the basin of attraction, quantified through the trapping probability over the inlet section and the probability density functions of the force components.

infographic.key_insight: Including the Basset-Boussinesq history force weakens particle trapping in a microfluidic T-junction vortex by pushing trajectories outward and downstream.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For particle handling and separation in microfluidic junctions, memory effects can materially change capture zones and should be included in design predictions.
method: Single-phase simulations of the square T-junction base flow at Re = 500 and 570
Integrated inertial particle force balance with drag, pressure-gradient, and Basset-Boussinesq history force
Used spectral proper orthogonal decomposition and basin-of-attraction analysis to quantify vortex breathing and trapping
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that the history force remains non-negligible across the tested density-ratio and Stokes-number ranges, reduces the trapping basin, and that phase-dependent trajectories at Re = 570 were evaluated via trapping probability and force-component PDFs.
infographic.watch_item: Results are based on idealized numerical flow and particle models, so real devices may differ if particle interactions, walls, or non-Newtonian effects are significant.
infographic.paper_title: Particle dynamics in a microfluidic T-junction vortex flow: the role of history force

title: Non intrusive parametric Reduced Order Models based on physics for incompressible flow
authors: Cyrille Allery, Claudine Beghein
abstract: Reduced order modeling provides an efficient alternative to high fidelity simulations for the rapid prediction of fluid flows in many query settings. Among non intrusive approaches, Operator Inference (OpInf) enables the identification of reduced dynamical operators directly from data while preserving a prescribed mathematical structure. The present work extends physics structured OpInf to the construction of parametric Reduced Order Models for transient incompressible flows governed by the Navier-Stokes equations. The velocity and pressure fields are represented using separate global reduced bases, and their reduced operators are identified directly from temporal and parametric POD coefficients. The identification procedure is formulated as a sequence of uncoupled least squares problems, leading to an efficient offline stage while avoiding the explicit projection of the governing equations. The approach is first evaluated on a lid driven cavity flow in a periodic regime to assess temporal extrapolation and prediction at previously unseen parameter values. Its applicability is then demonstrated for transient flow through a porous medium with a square obstacle, for which the nonlinear terms are not directly amenable to a standard Galerkin projection. The results demonstrate that the approach can accurately reproduce both velocity and pressure fields while providing computationally efficient predictions for unseen parameter values.

infographic.key_insight: Physics-structured, non-intrusive Operator Inference can learn parametric reduced models for incompressible Navier–Stokes flows directly from POD coefficients, without explicit projection of the full equations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables fast surrogate predictions of velocity and pressure for new operating conditions, supporting rapid design, control, and uncertainty studies in fluid systems.
method: Separate global POD bases are built for velocity and pressure.
Reduced operators are identified from temporal and parametric coefficients via uncoupled least-squares problems.
The framework preserves a prescribed physics-based structure while remaining non-intrusive.
infographic.evidence_signal: The method is validated on a lid-driven cavity and a porous-medium flow with a square obstacle, showing accurate reconstruction and prediction of velocity and pressure for unseen parameter values.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on the quality and coverage of training snapshots; extrapolation beyond the sampled temporal or parametric range may degrade accuracy.
infographic.paper_title: Non intrusive parametric Reduced Order Models based on physics for incompressible flow

title: Conjugate heat transfer in turbulent pipe flow with azimuthally non-uniform heating
authors: Jonathan Neuhauser, Davide Gatti, Bettina Frohnapfel
abstract: Turbulent conjugate heat transfer (CHT) in pipes with azimuthally non-uniform heating is studied theoretically and numerically with a focus on low-$\mathrm{Pr}$ fluids. While the influence of the solid properties is well documented for uniform heat flux, their effect under azimuthally non-uniform heating has not been explored systematically. We address this gap by combining spectral analysis of the problem -- which reduces arbitrary boundary conditions to a discrete set of azimuthal wavenumbers -- with well-resolved numerical simulations of thermally and hydraulically fully developed turbulent pipe flow at $\mathrm{Re}_τ\approx 180$ for $\mathrm{Pr} = \{0.025, 0.71\}$, representative of liquid metals and air. Two principal results emerge: (i) the global Nusselt number is independent of the azimuthal heat-flux distribution and exhibits only a minor dependence on the solid properties, resolving an open question for low-Prandtl-number fluids; (ii) CHT nevertheless strongly affects the azimuthally resolved mean temperature at low $\mathrm{Pr}$, where azimuthal conduction in the solid homogenises the interface heat flux, and governs the level of temperature fluctuations through the effusivity ratio (thermal activity ratio) $K$. Finally, an analysis of the turbulent Prandtl number $\mathrm{Pr}_{t}$ shows a strong anisotropy, particularly near the wall, and a dependence on the azimuthal wavenumber.

infographic.key_insight: In turbulent pipe flow with azimuthally non-uniform heating, the global Nusselt number is essentially unchanged by the azimuthal heat-flux pattern and only weakly affected by solid properties, but the local temperature field and fluctuations remain strongly shaped by conjugate heat transfer at low Prandtl number.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Designers of liquid-metal and other low-Prandtl-number cooling systems can rely on robust overall heat-transfer performance while still accounting for strong local thermal nonuniformity caused by the pipe wall and heat-flux distribution.
method: Spectral decomposition of arbitrary azimuthal heating into discrete wavenumbers.
Well-resolved thermally and hydraulically fully developed turbulent pipe-flow simulations.
Comparison across Pr = 0.025 and 0.71 with varying solid thermal properties and effusivity ratio K.
infographic.evidence_signal: The study combines theory with numerical simulations at Re_tau ≈ 180 and reports that the global Nusselt number is independent of azimuthal heat-flux distribution, while local mean temperature and fluctuations depend on wavenumber and solid coupling.
infographic.watch_item: The results are obtained for thermally and hydraulically fully developed flow at moderate Re_tau, so extrapolation to higher Reynolds numbers, transients, or strongly developing inlet conditions should be done cautiously.
infographic.paper_title: Conjugate heat transfer in turbulent pipe flow with azimuthally non-uniform heating

title: Geometric Mechanics of Real-Space Energy Transfer in Turbulence
authors: Weijie Zhang, Hanxun Yao
abstract: How the local energy transfer across scales in turbulence is encoded in the instantaneous deformation of fluid elements remains a fundamental question. We exploit the spherical geometry of the real-space energy cascade at length scale $\ell$. An exact derivation shows that it can be decomposed locally by strain self-amplification and vortex stretching, with a coefficient equal to the specific moment of inertia $2/5(\ell/2)^2$ of a spherical fluid neighborhood. Direct numerical simulations show that this contribution captures the dominant local transfer and defines a statistical boundary separating forward- and inverse-cascade events. A further longitudinal and transverse decomposition reveals that the longitudinal transfer underlying Kolmogorov's $4/5$ law is governed solely by strain self-amplification, whereas vortex stretching enters through the transverse component. These results establish a purely mechanical connection between turbulent energy cascade and the local rotational and deformational dynamics of fluid elements.

infographic.key_insight: Turbulent energy transfer at scale ℓ can be written as a local mechanical effect of strain self-amplification and vortex stretching, with a geometric coefficient tied to a spherical fluid neighborhood’s moment of inertia.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides a physically grounded way to diagnose and separate forward versus inverse cascade events in turbulence models, simulations, and flow-control analyses.
method: Derived an exact real-space cascade decomposition from spherical geometry at length scale ℓ.
Split local transfer into strain self-amplification and vortex-stretching contributions.
Further decomposed transfer into longitudinal and transverse components to isolate the mechanism behind the 4/5 law.
infographic.evidence_signal: Direct numerical simulations showed the derived contribution captures dominant local transfer and forms a statistical boundary between forward- and inverse-cascade events.
infographic.watch_item: The result is exact for the idealized spherical local geometry, so applying it in complex flows may require careful interpretation of scale selection and component decomposition.
infographic.paper_title: Geometric Mechanics of Real-Space Energy Transfer in Turbulence

title: Re-emergence of fingering in solidifying liquid-metal drops
authors: Siyu Zhang, Feng Wang, Yuan Ma, Hao Jiang, Kai Leong Chong, Quan Zhou
abstract: Solidification is expected to suppress fingering by removing mobile liquid. Here we report an unexpected re-emergence of fingering in impacting molten-tin drops: cooling first weakens peripheral fingers, but stronger undercooling restores them. At weak undercooling, fingers originate from a decelerating liquid rim and solidification reduces the effective acceleration that drives Rayleigh--Taylor-like amplification. At strong undercooling, solidification structures develop while liquid is still spreading, creating lateral mobility contrasts that redirect the residual flow. Comparison between the kinematically estimated solidification time and the experimentally measured fingering-onset and growth-termination times reveals a reversal in temporal ordering across the temperature range. A physics-based reduced-order model combines solidification-modified rim deceleration with mobility-gradient growth, captures the characteristic onset dynamics and accounts for the final finger length within the same physical framework.These findings establish solidification as an active means of regulating interfacial flow and morphology, with broad implications spanning metal-based additive manufacturing and debris mitigation in semiconducting industry.

infographic.key_insight: Solidification does not always suppress fingering in impacting molten-tin drops; beyond a threshold undercooling it can re-enable fingers by changing rim deceleration and creating mobility contrasts in the spreading liquid.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This offers a controllable route to tune splashing and morphology in metal droplet processes, relevant to additive manufacturing and semiconductor debris mitigation.
method: Experiments on impacting molten-tin drops across a range of undercooling levels
Physics-based reduced-order model coupling solidification-modified rim deceleration with mobility-gradient growth
Comparison of estimated solidification time with measured fingering onset and finger-growth termination
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a reversal in the timing between solidification and fingering across temperature, and the reduced-order model reproduces the onset dynamics and final finger length.
infographic.watch_item: The mechanism is derived for molten-tin drop impacts, so its transferability to other alloys, substrates, or impact conditions may require re-validation.
infographic.paper_title: Re-emergence of fingering in solidifying liquid-metal drops

title: Learning minimum-time navigation policies in two-dimensional flows with a genetic algorithm
authors: Vladimir Parfenyev
abstract: We study minimum-time navigation between two points in a known two-dimensional fluid flow for a vessel with fixed-magnitude slip velocity and controllable direction. The navigation policy is parameterized by a neural network and optimized using a genetic algorithm that evolves an ensemble of candidate strategies through Darwinian selection and parameter mutation, without crossover. The method recovers analytical and numerical optimal-control solutions in several benchmark cases, including two-dimensional turbulence, and outperforms Q-learning and one-step actor-critic method. We further show that the learned navigation strategies are robust to variations in the starting position and to unresolved small-scale turbulent fluctuations, provided that the characteristic velocity of these fluctuations remains small compared to the vessel's slip velocity. The proposed approach provides a compact representation of the navigation policy, is readily parallelizable, and eliminates the need for reward shaping, offering an efficient alternative to existing analytical and numerical methods for computing minimum-time trajectories in complex flows.

infographic.key_insight: A neural-network navigation policy optimized by a genetic algorithm can learn near-optimal minimum-time steering in 2D flows, matching analytical solutions and handling turbulent cases.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This offers a compact, parallelizable route-planning method for autonomous vehicles moving through complex fluids, with less manual reward design than reinforcement learning.
method: Encode the steering policy as a neural network mapping local state to control direction.
Use a genetic algorithm with selection and parameter mutation to evolve candidate policies; no crossover.
Benchmark against analytical/optimal-control solutions, Q-learning, and actor-critic methods in several 2D flow cases.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports recovery of analytical and numerical optima in benchmark problems, better performance than Q-learning and one-step actor-critic, and robustness to start-point variation and unresolved turbulence when fluctuation velocity is small.
infographic.watch_item: Robustness is conditional: unresolved turbulent fluctuations must remain weak relative to the vessel’s slip velocity, so performance may degrade in stronger subgrid variability.
infographic.paper_title: Learning minimum-time navigation policies in two-dimensional flows with a genetic algorithm

title: Predicting the Final Stationary State of Sheared 2D Euler Fluids
authors: Renato Pakter, Yan Levin
abstract: The Kelvin-Helmholtz (KH) instability is a fundamental signature of the natural world, manifesting in phenomena ranging from atmospheric clouds to the iconic turbulence of Jupiter's Great Red Spot. While the linear dynamics of this instability is well-understood, the ultimate fate of the fluid --- the final stationary state to which it relaxes --- remains a formidable challenge. In this paper, we present a general non-equilibrium statistical mechanics framework that allows us to predict the asymptotic vorticity distribution of a sheared 2D Euler fluid. By constructing a self-consistent ansatz for the solution of the Vlasov equation, we determine the stationary stream function without explicitly solving the time-dependent Euler equations. We demonstrate that the relaxation leads to a population-inverted core, where high-energy states are fully occupied, surrounded by a tenuous halo of vortices in the lower-energy regions of configuration space. This result establishes the core-halo structure as a robust statistical consequence of the system's evolution, offering a universal framework for understanding the saturation of shear-induced turbulence in inviscid 2D fluids.

infographic.key_insight: A self-consistent statistical mechanics model predicts the final stationary vorticity state of a sheared 2D Euler fluid, revealing a robust core-halo structure with a population-inverted core.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides a practical way to anticipate long-time shear-flow outcomes in inviscid 2D turbulence without directly simulating the full time-dependent Euler dynamics.
method: Build a self-consistent ansatz for the Vlasov equation.
Infer the stationary stream function from non-equilibrium statistical mechanics.
Predict the asymptotic vorticity distribution and resulting core-halo structure.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a theoretical demonstration of stationary-state prediction and a qualitative match to the expected relaxation outcome, rather than a data-driven benchmark.
infographic.watch_item: The framework appears tailored to idealized inviscid 2D Euler/Vlasov dynamics, so extending it to viscous, noisy, or fully 3D flows may require additional modeling.
infographic.paper_title: Predicting the Final Stationary State of Sheared 2D Euler Fluids

title: A nonclassical law of the wall in superfluid helium-4
authors: Mikai Hulse, Musfequs Salehin, Sosuke Inui, Wei Guo
abstract: The logarithmic law of the wall is one of the most robust scaling laws of classical turbulence, yet whether it survives in a quantum fluid such as superfluid $^4$He (He II) remains unknown. At a solid wall, the viscous normal-fluid and inviscid superfluid components of He II obey fundamentally different boundary conditions, yet their motions can be coupled through quantized vortices. How these competing effects organize the near-wall flow remains an open question in quantum-fluid hydrodynamics. Here we visualize the near-wall velocity field in mechanically driven He II pipe flows at Reynolds numbers up to $1.26\times10^6$ using molecular tagging velocimetry and independently determine the wall shear stress from pressure-drop measurements. We find that the normal-fluid velocity develops a robust logarithmic profile, showing that a law-of-the-wall description persists despite the two-fluid nature of He II. Strikingly, however, the resulting wall law is distinctly nonclassical: the effective Kármán constant is less than half its classical value and remains nearly unchanged across the temperature range studied. This invariance, despite substantial changes in the relative fractions of the two components, indicates strong dynamical coupling between them. These results not only reveal how a universal law of classical turbulence is transformed by quantum hydrodynamics, but also provide valuable guidance for the design and operation of cryogenic cooling systems involving He II transport.

infographic.key_insight: Superfluid helium-4 still exhibits a logarithmic law of the wall, but with a distinctly nonclassical, reduced Kármán constant that stays nearly temperature-invariant, implying strong coupling between the normal and superfluid components.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides a practical near-wall flow law for He II, helping improve the design and operation of cryogenic cooling and transport systems.
method: Molecular tagging velocimetry to visualize near-wall velocity in mechanically driven He II pipe flow
Independent wall-shear-stress estimation from pressure-drop measurements
Comparison of wall profiles across temperatures and Reynolds numbers up to 1.26×10^6
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports robust logarithmic velocity profiles in the normal-fluid component across the tested range, with a Kármán constant less than half the classical value and nearly unchanged with temperature.
infographic.watch_item: The observed wall law is specific to the measured pipe-flow regime and temperature range, so broader applicability to other geometries or flow states should be validated before use in design.
infographic.paper_title: A nonclassical law of the wall in superfluid helium-4

title: Machine-learning-assisted phase-amplitude reduction for fast synchronization of airfoil wakes with constrained fluctuations
authors: Daiki Beppu, Vedasri Godavarthi, Koichiro Yawata, Hiroya Nakao, Kai Fukami
abstract: This study considers rapidly modifying the wake shedding frequency of the flow around an airfoil using sparse sensor information, subject to constraints on the lift coefficient fluctuations. This is achieved by combining phase-amplitude reduction with nonlinear machine-learning-based sparse sensor reconstruction. We derive time-varying phase and amplitude sensitivity fields that identify the optimal spatial locations and timing for actuation from merely three sensors. Through the sensitivity fields, we analytically obtain the optimal waveform for fast synchronization of wake shedding frequency while minimizing amplitude deviation of aerodynamic responses. The proposed approach is evaluated using flows over various NACA airfoils at several post-stall angles of attack, all of which exhibit unsteady periodic vortex shedding. With the identified optimal forcing, the wake frequency is altered much faster than with a standard sinusoidal actuation. Furthermore, the amplitude-penalized forcing achieves $20\%$ suppression of the lift coefficient fluctuation compared to the optimal forcing without amplitude penalty. The current amplitude-penalized technique may offer an efficient path for fast flow modification without causing detrimental fluctuations in periodic aerodynamic and aeroelastic systems with fluid-structure interactions.

infographic.key_insight: By combining phase-amplitude reduction with sparse-sensor machine learning, the method rapidly retunes airfoil wake shedding while directly constraining lift fluctuations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This offers a practical control strategy for post-stall airfoils and other periodic flow systems where fast frequency shifting is needed without inducing harmful aerodynamic variability.
method: Reconstruct the wake state from only three sparse sensors using nonlinear machine-learning-based inference.
Compute time-varying phase and amplitude sensitivity fields to locate optimal actuation timing and spatial forcing.
Derive an optimal waveform that speeds synchronization while penalizing amplitude deviations in the lift response.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across several NACA airfoils at post-stall angles of attack, the optimized forcing changed wake frequency faster than standard sinusoidal actuation and reduced lift fluctuations by 20% with amplitude penalty.
infographic.watch_item: The approach depends on accurate sparse-sensor reconstruction and flow-specific sensitivity fields, so robustness may drop under strong noise, model mismatch, or off-design conditions.
infographic.paper_title: Machine-learning-assisted phase-amplitude reduction for fast synchronization of airfoil wakes with constrained fluctuations

title: Kinetic Reduction and Hydrodynamics under Time-Dependent Helical Symmetry
authors: Qingyun Zeng, Fan Feng
abstract: Translational and helical symmetries provide idealized descriptions of many flows encountered in nature and engineering. While translationally symmetric flows have been extensively studied within kinetic and continuum frameworks, the corresponding connection between microscopic dynamics and continuum behaviour for helical flows is less developed. Here, we investigate this connection for a dilute gas with time-dependent helical symmetry. Using the objective molecular dynamics framework, we derive a reduced Boltzmann equation that retains radial variations while preserving the classical collision operator under helical symmetry. Formal hydrodynamic expansions then yield the corresponding Euler and Navier-Stokes-Fourier equations. The resulting models describe how cylindrical geometry and axial deformation influence transport, including viscous transport and heat conduction, and how deformation generates unequal stresses along and across the axis in competition with collisional relaxation. Comparisons with direct simulation Monte Carlo solutions examine both spatially uniform and radially varying flows. In the cases studied, the first-order fluid corrections capture the leading stress anisotropy and improve the prediction of radial temperature variations, while larger Knudsen numbers expose limitations of the approximation.

infographic.key_insight: The paper derives a reduced kinetic-to-fluid description for dilute gases with time-dependent helical symmetry, showing how geometry and deformation create anisotropic stresses and transport effects.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It provides a more physically faithful model for predicting flow, stress, and temperature in helical or cylindrical devices where axial deformation and heat transfer matter.
method: Derives a reduced Boltzmann equation that keeps radial variation while preserving the classical collision operator.
Uses formal hydrodynamic expansion to obtain Euler and Navier–Stokes–Fourier equations under helical symmetry.
Compares the reduced models against direct simulation Monte Carlo for uniform and radially varying flows.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that first-order fluid corrections capture leading stress anisotropy and improve radial temperature prediction in the tested cases.
infographic.watch_item: Accuracy degrades at larger Knudsen numbers, so the continuum closure may miss stronger rarefaction effects.
infographic.paper_title: Kinetic Reduction and Hydrodynamics under Time-Dependent Helical Symmetry

title: Conditional Flow Matching for Generation of 3D Multi-variable Instantaneous Urban Microclimate Fields
authors: Peng Liu, Shaoxiang Qin, Theodore Potsis, Lili Ji, Dingyang Geng, Liangzhu Leon Wang
abstract: Rapid and accurate prediction of urban wind and temperature fields is important for urban microclimate design and climate adaptation. Large-eddy simulation (LES) effectively resolves these instantaneous fields, but its application is limited in iterative design of urban microclimate applications due to high computational cost. Existing regressive data-driven models offers quick outputs, but they produce only deterministic point predictions that inherently fail to represent turbulent stochasticity. This paper adopts a novel generative framework of Conditional Flow Matching (CFM) that uses building geometry and mean flow as guidance to generate plausible three-dimensional instantaneous velocity and temperature fields for urban microclimate in seconds. To overcome the GPU memory bottleneck of pixel space 3D generation, the model operates in parallel on overlapping pixel space through a shared-noise initialization that preserves high spatial continuity of flow structure across the entire domain. Against reference LES data, the CFM surrogate can rapidly and accurately restore the first-order statistics with Normalized Root Mean Square Error (NRMSE) of 2.99% for wind and 1.77% for temperature, second-order turbulence metrics with NRMSE of 7.17% for wind and 8.84% for temperature, turbulent kinetic energy with NRMSE of 7%, probability density function and vertical profiles in representative locations. Wind engineering application of local gust prediction demonstrate that the speed and accuracy of CFM, supporting the use of generative AI for making turbulence-aware resilient urban design and climate adaptation more computationally feasible.

infographic.key_insight: A conditional flow-matching generative model can rapidly synthesize plausible 3D urban wind and temperature fields from building geometry and mean flow, capturing turbulent variability rather than only deterministic averages.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables near-real-time, turbulence-aware urban microclimate assessment for design iteration, local gust analysis, and climate-adaptation planning without repeated expensive LES runs.
method: Uses Conditional Flow Matching as a generative surrogate conditioned on urban geometry and mean flow.
Generates 3D instantaneous velocity and temperature fields in pixel space.
Mitigates GPU memory limits by running on overlapping subdomains with shared-noise initialization to preserve continuity.
infographic.evidence_signal: Compared with LES, the model reported low NRMSE for first-order statistics (2.99% wind, 1.77% temperature) and good agreement for turbulence metrics, TKE, PDFs, and vertical profiles.
infographic.watch_item: Pixel-space 3D generation with subdomain stitching may be sensitive to boundary consistency and memory constraints, so domain decomposition and continuity handling must be implemented carefully.
infographic.paper_title: Conditional Flow Matching for Generation of 3D Multi-variable Instantaneous Urban Microclimate Fields
